questions.question: Compare binary trees and binary search trees in Java. Cover their properties, time complexity for operations, and when each is used.
questions.title: Binary Tree vs Binary Search Tree in Java — Properties, Complexity, Use Cases
questions.direct_answer: A **binary tree** is any tree where each node has **at most two children** (left, right) — no ordering constraint. A **binary search tree (BST)** is a binary tree with the **BST property**: for every node, all keys in the **left subtree are smaller**, all keys in the **right subtree are larger** (and equal keys typically go right or are disallowed). **Operations**: **Binary tree** — search/insert/delete are **O(n)** (must scan all nodes); used for **hierarchical structures** (expression trees, decision trees, file systems represented as binary trees, heaps as a special case). **BST** — search/insert/delete are **O(log n) average** (balanced) but **O(n) worst case** (degenerate / skewed when input is sorted); used for **ordered key-value storage** with fast lookup, range queries, and in-order traversal that yields sorted output. **Self-balancing BSTs** (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee **O(log n) worst case** by rebalancing after each insert/delete — Java's `TreeMap` and `TreeSet` use Red-Black trees. **In Java**: there's no built-in plain binary tree; you implement nodes manually (`class Node { int val; Node left, right; }`). For BST behavior, use **`TreeMap`** (key-value), **`TreeSet`** (keys only), or **`PriorityQueue`** (heap, partial ordering). **When to use each**: **Binary tree** for hierarchies and expressions; **BST** when you need ordered storage with O(log n) ops and in-order iteration; **balanced BST** (TreeMap/TreeSet) when you need worst-case guarantees; **HashMap/HashSet** for unordered O(1) average lookup (no in-order traversal); **PriorityQueue** when you only need min/max access. **Common bug**: implementing a BST without balancing → worst-case O(n) on sorted input.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate distinguishes a binary tree from a BST, knows the BST property, average vs worst-case complexity, and the role of self-balancing in TreeMap/TreeSet
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying BST is always O(log n) (only for balanced). Confusing binary tree with BST. Not knowing TreeMap is a Red-Black tree. Forgetting in-order traversal yields sorted output for BSTs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention self-balancing variants (AVL, Red-Black, B-tree), discuss the worst-case skew problem, address Java's TreeMap as Red-Black, mention heap as a special-case binary tree, contrast BST vs HashMap trade-offs

sections.title: Binary Tree vs Binary Search Tree — Side by Side
sections.content:
| Property | Binary Tree | Binary Search Tree (BST) |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | Each node has ≤ 2 children | Binary tree + BST property |
| **Ordering constraint** | None | left < node < right |
| **Search** | O(n) | O(log n) avg / O(n) worst |
| **Insert** | O(1) at known position; O(n) to find | O(log n) avg / O(n) worst |
| **Delete** | O(1) given parent ref; O(n) to find | O(log n) avg / O(n) worst |
| **In-order traversal** | Arbitrary order | **Sorted order** (key property) |
| **Use case** | Expression tree, file hierarchy | Ordered storage, range queries |
| **Worst-case shape** | Linear chain (intentional) | Linear chain (degenerate, bug) |
| **Java built-in** | None (DIY) | TreeMap/TreeSet (Red-Black) |
| **Self-balancing variants** | N/A | AVL, Red-Black, Splay, B-tree |
| **Predecessor / successor** | O(n) | O(log n) avg |
| **Range query** | O(n) | O(log n + k) for k results |

sections.title: Binary Tree — Plain, No Ordering
Binary Search Tree — Ordered, O(log n) Average
Self-Balancing BSTs — Why They Matter
sections.content:
**Problem**: a plain BST can degenerate to a linked list, making operations O(n). Self-balancing BSTs **rotate** subtrees during insert/delete to maintain a height bound of **O(log n)**.

**AVL Tree** (Adelson-Velsky & Landis, 1962):
- Strict balance: heights of left and right subtrees differ by at most 1.
- Rotations: single (LL, RR), double (LR, RL).
- Time: O(log n) for all operations, **strict guarantee**.
- Use case: **lookup-heavy workloads** (stricter balance → faster searches).

**Red-Black Tree** (Bayer 1972, Guibas & Sedgewick 1978):
- Looser balance: each path from root to leaf has the same number of 'black' nodes; height ≤ 2 · log₂(n+1).
- Fewer rotations on insert/delete than AVL.
- Time: O(log n) for all operations.
- Use case: **mixed read/write workloads**; Java's `TreeMap`, `TreeSet`, `HashMap` (treeified buckets), Linux scheduler, .NET SortedDictionary.

**B-Tree / B+ Tree**:
- Multi-way (N-ary) balanced tree, not binary.
- Each node holds many keys; reduces tree height for disk-resident data.
- Use case: databases (B+ tree indexes in PostgreSQL, MySQL), file systems (NTFS, HFS+).

**Splay Tree**:
- Recently accessed nodes move toward root via splaying rotations.
- Amortized O(log n).
- Use case: caches (recently accessed = frequently accessed).

**Treap**:
- BST + heap on random priorities; expected O(log n).
- Simpler to implement than AVL/Red-Black.

**Java's choice: Red-Black tree**
- Used in `TreeMap`, `TreeSet`, and `HashMap` (when buckets exceed 8 entries; treeification since Java 8).
- Good balance of read and write performance.
- Implementation in `java.util.TreeMap`.

sections.title: When to Use Which
sections.content:
**Plain binary tree**: when you have a **hierarchical structure** with no inherent order.
```java
// Expression tree for (a + b) * c
TreeNode root = new TreeNode('*');
root.left = new TreeNode('+');
root.left.left = new TreeNode('a');
root.left.right = new TreeNode('b');
root.right = new TreeNode('c');
```

**Plain BST**: rare in production. Use only if you know input is random/balanced and don't need worst-case guarantees. For interviews: implement to demonstrate understanding.

**TreeMap / TreeSet (Red-Black BST)**: when you need:
- **Ordered iteration** (`firstKey`, `lastKey`, `subMap`, `headMap`, `tailMap`).
- **Range queries** (`ceilingKey`, `floorKey`, `higherKey`, `lowerKey`).
- **Worst-case O(log n)** for all operations.
- **Sorted iteration**.
```java
TreeMap<Integer, String> map = new TreeMap<>();
map.put(5, "five");
map.put(3, "three");
map.put(7, "seven");
map.firstKey();         // 3
map.ceilingKey(4);      // 5 (smallest >= 4)
map.subMap(3, 7);       // {3=three, 5=five}
```

**HashMap / HashSet**: when you need:
- **Unordered** O(1) average lookup/insert/delete.
- No range queries or ordered iteration.
- Faster than TreeMap for lookups.

**PriorityQueue (heap)**: when you need:
- **Min or max** access in O(1), insert/extract in O(log n).
- Don't need full ordering, only min/max access.
- Examples: Dijkstra's algorithm, top-K, scheduling.

**LinkedHashMap**: when you need:
- O(1) average lookup AND insertion-order iteration.
- LRU cache implementation.

**Decision matrix**:
- **Order matters + range queries**: TreeMap.
- **Order matters + insertion order**: LinkedHashMap.
- **Lookup speed only**: HashMap.
- **Min/max only**: PriorityQueue.
- **Hierarchical data**: plain binary tree (or N-ary).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Binary tree**: each node has ≤ 2 children; no ordering.
- **BST**: binary tree + property: left < node < right.
- **In-order traversal of BST yields sorted output** — defining property.
- **Plain BST**: O(log n) average, **O(n) worst case** (skewed/degenerate).
- **Self-balancing BSTs** (AVL, Red-Black): O(log n) worst case.
- **Java's TreeMap, TreeSet**: Red-Black trees.
- **Java's HashMap**: uses Red-Black for treeified buckets (≥ 8 entries) since Java 8.
- **No built-in plain binary tree** in Java — implement yourself.
- **Use cases for binary tree**: expression trees, decision trees, file hierarchies, Huffman coding, heaps, ASTs.
- **Use cases for BST**: ordered storage, range queries, sorted iteration.
- **Range query on BST**: O(log n + k) for k results.
- **Predecessor / successor**: O(log n) on balanced BST.
- **HashMap vs TreeMap**: HashMap O(1) avg, no order; TreeMap O(log n), sorted.
- **PriorityQueue**: heap (special binary tree); only min or max access in O(log n).
- **AVL vs Red-Black**: AVL stricter balance (faster reads); Red-Black fewer rotations (faster writes); Red-Black is the common choice.
- **B-tree**: multi-way variant for disk-resident data (databases, file systems).
- **For interviews**: implement BST insert/search/delete; explain in-order traversal yielding sorted output; mention self-balancing for worst-case guarantees.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Binary tree vs BST — the difference**

**Binary tree**
- Each node has at most 2 children
- No ordering constraint
- Just a structural concept

**Binary search tree (BST)**
- Binary tree + BST property
- Left subtree all < node
- Right subtree all > node

**The defining property of BST**
- In-order traversal yields sorted output
- (left, node, right) recursively → ascending order

**Operations**

**Binary tree**
- Search: O(n) — must check every node
- Insert/delete: O(1) given position, O(n) to find
- Used when structure matters, not order

**BST**
- Search/insert/delete: O(log n) average
- O(n) WORST CASE if skewed
- Predecessor/successor: O(log n) avg
- Range query: O(log n + k)

**The skew problem**
- Insert sorted data 1,2,3,4,5 into plain BST
- All right children → linked list
- Operations degrade to O(n)
- Solution: self-balancing trees

**Self-balancing BSTs**

**AVL**
- Strict balance (height diff ≤ 1)
- Faster lookups
- More rotations on writes

**Red-Black**
- Looser balance (height ≤ 2 log n)
- Fewer rotations on writes
- Mixed workloads
- **Java's choice for TreeMap, TreeSet**

**B-tree / B+ tree**
- Multi-way, not binary
- Disk-resident data
- Databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL indexes)

**Splay tree**
- Recently-accessed moves to root
- Amortized O(log n)
- Caches

**Java built-ins**

**No plain binary tree** — implement yourself
```java
class Node { int val; Node left, right; }
```

**TreeMap / TreeSet** — Red-Black BST
- O(log n) all operations
- Range queries: ceilingKey, floorKey, subMap
- Sorted iteration

**HashMap (treeified buckets)** — since Java 8
- Bucket has linked list normally
- Converts to Red-Black tree when bucket size > 8
- Mitigates worst-case hash collisions

**PriorityQueue** — binary heap
- Special complete binary tree
- O(1) peek, O(log n) insert/extract
- For min/max access only, not full order

**Use cases**

**Plain binary tree**
- Expression trees: (a+b)*c
- Decision trees
- File hierarchies
- Huffman coding
- Heaps (special case)
- Abstract syntax trees
- Game trees (minimax)

**BST (TreeMap/TreeSet)**
- Ordered storage
- Range queries
- Sorted iteration
- Worst-case O(log n) guarantees

**HashMap**
- Unordered O(1) avg
- No range queries
- Faster than TreeMap for lookups

**LinkedHashMap**
- O(1) avg + insertion order
- LRU cache

**PriorityQueue**
- Min/max access only
- Dijkstra, top-K, scheduling

**Decision matrix**

- Order + range queries → TreeMap
- Order + insertion order → LinkedHashMap
- Lookup speed only → HashMap
- Min/max only → PriorityQueue
- Hierarchical data → plain binary tree

**Tree shapes**

**Full binary tree**
- Every node has 0 or 2 children

**Complete binary tree**
- All levels full except possibly last
- Last level filled left-to-right
- Heaps are complete

**Perfect binary tree**
- All internals have 2 children
- All leaves at same depth

**Balanced binary tree**
- Left and right subtree heights differ by ≤ 1

**Common bugs**

**1. Not balancing**
- Plain BST + sorted input → O(n)
- Use TreeMap, not custom BST

**2. Confusing binary tree with BST**
- Binary tree has no order
- BST has order

**3. Forgetting in-order traversal property**
- BST in-order = sorted output
- Use this to validate a BST or to sort

**4. Implementing delete incorrectly**
- Three cases: leaf, one child, two children
- For two children: replace with in-order successor

**5. Not knowing TreeMap is Red-Black**
- It's not just 'a sorted map' — it's a Red-Black tree
- O(log n) worst case guaranteed

**For interviews**
- Define binary tree vs BST clearly
- Mention in-order traversal yields sorted output
- Discuss skew → self-balancing
- Address Java's TreeMap as Red-Black
- Contrast with HashMap (no order, O(1) avg)

**Recommendation:** A **binary tree** is any tree where each node has at most 2 children — no ordering constraint, used for **hierarchical structures** like expression trees, decision trees, file systems, Huffman coding, heaps, and ASTs. A **binary search tree (BST)** adds the **BST property** (left < node < right), making search/insert/delete **O(log n) average** — but **O(n) worst case** if the tree degenerates into a chain (sorted input is the classic trigger). The defining property of a BST is that **in-order traversal yields sorted output**, which is invaluable for sorted iteration and range queries. **Self-balancing BSTs** (AVL, Red-Black, B-tree) maintain O(log n) worst case via rotations. **Java's `TreeMap`, `TreeSet`, and treeified HashMap buckets** all use **Red-Black trees** — chosen for fewer rotations than AVL while still providing O(log n) guarantees. **In Java**, you implement plain binary trees yourself (no built-in), but use **`TreeMap`/`TreeSet`** for ordered storage, **`HashMap`/`HashSet`** for unordered O(1) average lookups, **`LinkedHashMap`** for O(1) lookups with insertion-order iteration, and **`PriorityQueue`** for min/max access only. **Don't roll your own BST** in production — it's a classic source of O(n) worst-case bugs; use `TreeMap`/`TreeSet`. The mental model: **binary tree = hierarchy; BST = ordered hierarchy with O(log n) ops; balanced BST = guaranteed O(log n)**. Choose Red-Black (TreeMap) for general-purpose ordered storage, AVL for read-heavy workloads, B-tree/B+ tree for disk-resident data (databases), and heap for min/max-only access.

questions.question: Implement DFS tree traversals in Java — inorder, preorder, postorder — both recursively and iteratively with a stack.
questions.title: Tree Traversals in Java — Inorder, Preorder, Postorder (Recursive and Iterative)
questions.direct_answer: **DFS tree traversals** visit each node once, ordered by when the node is processed relative to its children. **Three orders**: **Preorder** (Root, Left, Right) — visit node first; used for **copying a tree**, serializing, prefix expression. **Inorder** (Left, Root, Right) — used for **BSTs** (yields sorted order), printing expression in infix. **Postorder** (Left, Right, Root) — visit node last; used for **deleting a tree** (free children before parent), evaluating postfix expression, computing tree-aggregate values like height. **All are O(n) time** (visit every node) and **O(h) space** for recursion (h = height; O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed). **Recursive versions** are short and natural; **iterative versions** use an explicit `Deque` (stack) and avoid stack overflow for very deep trees. **Iterative inorder**: push left children to stack, pop, visit, move to right child, repeat. **Iterative preorder**: push root, then in loop pop, visit, push right child first then left (so left is processed first). **Iterative postorder**: trickier — either use two stacks (modified preorder reversed) or track visited state per node. **Morris traversal**: O(1) extra space using threaded BST tricks; advanced. **Level-order (BFS)**: not DFS, uses a queue. For interviews: know all three recursive forms cold; iterative inorder and preorder are common; iterative postorder is advanced. **Common bug**: pushing children in wrong order in iterative preorder (right first, then left, so left comes off first).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can write all three traversals recursively, knows the iterative versions with an explicit stack, and understands when each is useful (inorder for BSTs, postorder for deletion)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrong iterative push order. Confusing inorder/preorder. Not handling null. Forgetting to mark visited in iterative postorder. Using recursion for a 10M-node tree (stack overflow)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Morris traversal (O(1) space), use cases for each order, contrast iterative vs recursive trade-offs, mention level-order (BFS) for completeness, and the visit-children-before-parent intuition for postorder

sections.title: Recursive Traversals — The Natural Form
Iterative Preorder — Stack-Based
Iterative Inorder — Walk-Left-Then-Right
Iterative Postorder — Two Approaches
Use Cases for Each Order
Morris Traversal — O(1) Space
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three DFS orders**: preorder (Root, L, R), inorder (L, Root, R), postorder (L, R, Root).
- **Mnemonic**: name describes WHEN root is visited (pre = before, in = between, post = after).
- **Time**: O(n) for all.
- **Space (recursive)**: O(h) recursion stack — O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.
- **Recursive versions** are short and natural — use unless stack overflow risk.
- **Iterative versions** use explicit `Deque` (stack); use `ArrayDeque`, not legacy `Stack`.
- **Iterative preorder**: push root, then pop-print-push (right first, then left).
- **Iterative inorder**: walk-left-push-then-pop-and-go-right pattern.
- **Iterative postorder**: two-stack trick (modified preorder + reverse) or single-stack with visited tracking.
- **Morris traversal**: O(1) extra space using threading; modifies tree temporarily.
- **Level-order (BFS)**: uses a queue, not DFS.
- **Inorder of BST yields sorted output** — critical property.
- **Postorder for deletion** (free children before parent) and aggregates (compute children before parent).
- **Preorder for copy / serialization**.
- **Common bugs**: wrong push order in iterative preorder, infinite loop in Morris (forgetting thread restoration), null node not handled.
- **For interviews**: know all 3 recursive cold; iterative inorder/preorder is common; iterative postorder advanced.
- **JVM stack limit**: ~10K-50K frames typical; for deeper trees use iterative or Morris.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Three DFS tree traversals**

**Preorder (Root, Left, Right)**
- Visit node first
- Recurse left, then right

**Inorder (Left, Root, Right)**
- Recurse left first
- Visit node
- Recurse right

**Postorder (Left, Right, Root)**
- Recurse left, then right
- Visit node last

**Mnemonic**: name says when ROOT is visited.
- Pre = before children
- In = between left and right
- Post = after children

**Recursive form (clean and natural)**
```java
void inorder(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return;
    inorder(node.left);
    visit(node);
    inorder(node.right);
}
```
- Time: O(n)
- Space: O(h) recursion stack

**Iterative preorder**
- Use Deque (ArrayDeque, not legacy Stack)
- Push root
- Loop: pop, visit, push right FIRST, then left
- (LIFO: left pops first)

**Iterative inorder**
- Walk left, push each node
- When null, pop and visit
- Move to right child of popped
- Repeat

**Iterative postorder — trickier**

**Approach 1: Two stacks**
- Modified preorder: Root, Right, Left
- Push to output stack (reversed)
- Pop output → postorder

**Approach 2: Single stack with visited tracking**
- Peek top
- If has unvisited right, descend
- Else visit and pop
- Track lastVisited to avoid re-descending

**Use cases for each order**

**Preorder**
- Copy tree (root before children)
- Serialize tree
- Prefix expression
- DFS path enumeration

**Inorder**
- BST sorted output (THE key property)
- Validate BST (should be strictly increasing)
- K-th smallest in BST
- Infix expression printing

**Postorder**
- Delete tree (free children first)
- Evaluate postfix
- Compute height (need children's heights)
- Compute aggregates (sum, count)
- Topological sort (reverse postorder of DAG)

**Level-order (BFS)**
- Not DFS, uses queue
- Level-by-level
- Shortest path in unweighted tree

**Morris traversal — O(1) space**
- Thread the tree temporarily
- For each node with left child, find rightmost in left subtree (predecessor)
- Set pred.right = current to create thread
- On revisit, restore and visit
- Time O(n), space O(1)
- Modifies tree temporarily; not thread-safe
- Advanced; mention in interviews if relevant

**Common bugs**

**1. Wrong iterative push order**
- Iterative preorder: push RIGHT first, then LEFT
- Stack is LIFO; left pops first
- Common mistake: push left then right → wrong order

**2. Confusing inorder and preorder**
- Practice all three until automatic

**3. Not handling null**
- Recursive: `if (node == null) return;`
- Iterative: check before pushing

**4. Iterative postorder errors**
- Forgetting visited tracking → infinite loop
- Two-stack version is easier; use it if approach 2 is shaky

**5. Stack overflow on deep trees**
- JVM default ~10K-50K stack frames
- Skewed BST or linked-list tree can overflow
- Use iterative or Morris

**6. Using legacy Stack class**
- Synchronized, slow
- Use ArrayDeque

**Interviews — what to know**

**Recursive**: all 3, cold
**Iterative inorder**: walk-left-push pattern
**Iterative preorder**: pop, push right then left
**Iterative postorder**: two-stack trick (or single-stack with visited)
**Use cases**: in-order for BSTs, post-order for deletion
**BFS**: queue-based, level-by-level
**Morris**: O(1) space, advanced

**Practical tip**

**Use recursion** unless trees are very deep or you're avoiding stack overhead.

**Use iterative** for production code on user-supplied data (deep trees possible).

**Use Morris** only when O(1) space is critical and tree mutation is acceptable.

**Recommendation:** Master **all three DFS traversals** in both recursive and iterative forms. The **recursive versions** are short and natural — the order in the name (pre/in/post) tells you when the **root** is visited relative to children. Use them unless you have very deep trees (>10K depth) where stack overflow is a risk. The **iterative versions** use an explicit `Deque` (use **`ArrayDeque`**, not the legacy `Stack` class). **Iterative preorder** is the simplest — push root, then pop-visit-push-right-then-left (right first because the stack is LIFO and left should pop first). **Iterative inorder** uses a walk-left-push-then-pop pattern. **Iterative postorder** is the trickiest — the cleanest approach is to do a **modified preorder (Root, Right, Left)** pushing to an output stack, then pop the output stack to get the postorder. Know the **use cases**: **inorder for BSTs** (yields sorted output, validates BSTs, finds K-th smallest), **postorder for deletion and aggregates** (need children processed before parent), **preorder for copying and serialization**. Mention **level-order (BFS)** with a queue for completeness. For senior interviews, know **Morris traversal** — O(n) time, **O(1) extra space** by temporarily threading the tree. The mental model: **DFS = recursive descent + visit at one of three points; iterative = explicit stack mimicking the call stack**. Always handle null, choose `ArrayDeque` over `Stack`, and prefer recursive unless depth is a concern.

questions.question: Compare BFS and DFS in Java. Cover their complexity, memory usage, when to use each, and provide implementations for trees and graphs.
questions.title: BFS vs DFS in Java — Complexity, Memory, Use Cases
questions.direct_answer: **BFS (Breadth-First Search)** explores nodes **level by level** from the source, using a **queue (FIFO)**. **DFS (Depth-First Search)** explores **as deep as possible** before backtracking, using a **stack (LIFO)** — either explicit or implicit via recursion. Both are **O(V + E)** time for graphs, **O(n)** for trees. **Memory**: BFS O(W) where W = max width of any level (could be O(n) for wide trees); DFS O(H) where H = depth (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed/path-graph). **Use BFS when**: (1) finding **shortest path in unweighted graph**, (2) finding **minimum number of steps**, (3) **level-order traversal**, (4) finding all nodes within distance K, (5) **bipartite check**, (6) the answer is likely shallow. **Use DFS when**: (1) **path enumeration** (find any/all paths), (2) **cycle detection**, (3) **topological sort** (reverse postorder), (4) **connected components**, (5) **strongly connected components** (Tarjan/Kosaraju), (6) **maze solving / backtracking**, (7) the answer is likely deep, (8) memory is constrained for narrow tall trees. **Java implementations**: BFS uses `Queue<T>` (typically `ArrayDeque`); DFS uses `Deque<T>` (stack) or recursion. **For graphs**: both need a `visited` set to avoid cycles. **For trees**: no cycles, but DFS may revisit if you're not careful with parent pointers in N-ary trees. **Common variants**: **BFS shortest path** (track distance and parent), **DFS topological sort** (postorder of DAG, reversed), **bidirectional BFS** (search from both ends; meets in middle, much faster for shortest path in huge graphs), **iterative deepening DFS** (DFS with limit, repeated with increasing depth — BFS-like memory with DFS-like behavior).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the data structures (queue vs stack), complexity, memory trade-offs, and the right algorithm for shortest path, cycle detection, topological sort, etc.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying BFS uses stack and DFS uses queue (reversed). Forgetting visited set in graph traversal. Using BFS for unweighted shortest path but not tracking distance. Using DFS for shortest path (it doesn't give shortest)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss bidirectional BFS, iterative deepening DFS, BFS for level-order, DFS for topological sort, memory characteristics of wide vs tall graphs, and Dijkstra as 'BFS with priority queue for weighted graphs'

sections.title: BFS vs DFS — Side by Side
sections.content:
| Property | BFS | DFS |
|---|---|---|
| **Data structure** | Queue (FIFO) | Stack (LIFO) or recursion |
| **Order** | Level by level | Branch by branch |
| **Time** | O(V + E) graph; O(n) tree | O(V + E) graph; O(n) tree |
| **Space** | O(W), W = max width | O(H), H = max depth |
| **Shortest path (unweighted)** | **Yes** | No |
| **Path enumeration** | Awkward | **Natural** |
| **Cycle detection** | Yes (color/visited) | **Yes (back edges)** |
| **Topological sort** | Possible (Kahn's) | **Natural (reverse postorder)** |
| **Connected components** | Yes | **Natural** |
| **Memory for wide tree** | O(n) (worst) | O(log n) (balanced) |
| **Memory for skewed tree** | O(1) | O(n) |
| **Best when** | Answer near source | Path-finding, exhaustive search |
| **Risk** | OOM on wide graphs | Stack overflow on deep recursion |

sections.title: BFS — Queue-Based, Level by Level
DFS — Stack or Recursion, Branch by Branch
When to Use Which
sections.content:
**Use BFS when**:
- **Shortest path in unweighted graph or tree**: BFS guarantees minimum hops.
- **Find minimum number of steps to reach target**: word ladder, transformation problems.
- **Level-order traversal**: print tree level by level.
- **Find all nodes within distance K**: stop BFS at depth K.
- **Bipartite check**: alternate colors level-by-level.
- **Web crawler within N hops**.
- **Connected components in undirected graph** (either works, BFS more memory-friendly for narrow components).

**Use DFS when**:
- **Path enumeration**: find any/all paths from A to B.
- **Cycle detection**: back-edge detection in DFS tree.
- **Topological sort of DAG**: reverse postorder.
- **Strongly connected components**: Tarjan's, Kosaraju's algorithms.
- **Maze solving**: classic backtracking is DFS.
- **Tree problems**: subtree sums, heights, lowest common ancestor.
- **Memory-constrained on tall narrow graphs**.
- **Articulation points / bridges**: use DFS lowlink.
- **Backtracking** (N-queens, Sudoku, combinations).

**Don't use DFS for shortest path**: DFS finds **a** path, not the shortest. Even on unweighted graphs.

**For weighted shortest path**: use **Dijkstra's algorithm** (BFS with priority queue) for non-negative weights, or **Bellman-Ford** for negative weights.

**Memory considerations**:
- **Wide graph (e.g., binary tree)**: BFS holds up to n/2 nodes at the last level — O(n) memory.
- **Tall narrow graph (e.g., linked list)**: DFS recursion depth = n — O(n) stack.
- **Balanced tree**: BFS O(n/2), DFS O(log n) — DFS wins for memory.
- **Skewed tree**: BFS O(1) per level, DFS O(n) recursion — BFS wins.

**Mnemonic**:
- **Shortest path** → BFS.
- **Find any path / cycle / structure** → DFS.
- **Levels matter** → BFS.
- **Backtracking** → DFS.

sections.title: Advanced Variants
sections.content:
**Bidirectional BFS**: search from both source and target; meet in middle.
- Time: O(b^(d/2)) instead of O(b^d), where b = branching factor, d = distance.
- Memory: half of regular BFS (each search is shallower).
- Use case: shortest path in huge graph (e.g., social network).

**Iterative Deepening DFS (IDDFS)**:
- DFS with depth limit, repeated with limit = 1, 2, 3, ...
- BFS-like behavior (finds shortest first) with DFS memory.
- Time: O(b^d) (same as BFS), memory: O(d).
- Use case: very large search spaces (chess, puzzle games).

**0-1 BFS**: BFS variant for graphs with edge weights only 0 or 1. Use a deque — push 0-weight edges to front, 1-weight to back. O(V + E).

**A* search**: BFS + heuristic. f(n) = g(n) + h(n) where g = cost so far, h = estimated remaining. Optimal if h is admissible.

**Dijkstra's algorithm**: BFS with priority queue for non-negative weighted shortest path. O((V + E) log V).

**Bellman-Ford**: shortest path with negative weights. O(V · E). Detects negative cycles.

**Floyd-Warshall**: all-pairs shortest path. O(V³). Use when V is small.

**Multi-source BFS**: start BFS from multiple sources simultaneously. Useful for 'closest of any source' problems.

**Tarjan's SCC**: DFS-based. O(V + E) to find strongly connected components.

**Kosaraju's SCC**: two DFS passes. Conceptually simpler than Tarjan's.

**For interviews**: know BFS for shortest path, DFS for cycle / topo / paths. Mention bidirectional BFS or A* for large graphs.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **BFS**: queue (FIFO), level by level, finds shortest in unweighted.
- **DFS**: stack (LIFO) or recursion, branch by branch, exhaustive search.
- **Both O(V + E)** time for graphs, O(n) for trees.
- **Memory**: BFS O(W) max width, DFS O(H) max height.
- **For trees**: BFS = level-order; DFS = preorder/inorder/postorder.
- **For graphs**: both need `visited` set to avoid cycles.
- **Use ArrayDeque** for both queue and stack — faster than LinkedList or legacy Stack.
- **BFS finds shortest path** in unweighted graph — DFS does not.
- **DFS for path enumeration, cycle detection, topo sort, connected components, backtracking**.
- **Cycle detection (directed)**: 3-color DFS — back edge to GRAY = cycle.
- **Topological sort**: DFS postorder reversed (or Kahn's BFS).
- **Memory wins**:
  - Balanced tree: DFS O(log n) < BFS O(n).
  - Skewed: BFS O(1) < DFS O(n).
- **Bidirectional BFS**: O(b^(d/2)) for shortest path; meets in middle.
- **IDDFS**: BFS-like behavior, DFS-like memory.
- **Dijkstra**: BFS + priority queue for weighted shortest path (non-negative).
- **Bellman-Ford**: weighted shortest path with negative weights.
- **For DAG: topological sort + relaxation = O(V + E) shortest path**.
- **Stack overflow risk** for recursive DFS on deep graphs (~10K+); use iterative.
- **OOM risk** for BFS on wide graphs (millions of nodes per level); use bidirectional or limit.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**BFS vs DFS — the difference**

**BFS (Breadth-First Search)**
- Queue (FIFO)
- Level by level
- Finds shortest path in unweighted graph

**DFS (Depth-First Search)**
- Stack (LIFO) or recursion
- As deep as possible, then backtrack
- Path enumeration, cycle detection

**Both O(V + E)** for graphs, O(n) for trees.

**Memory**
- BFS: O(W) max width
- DFS: O(H) max depth
- Wide tree: DFS wins (O(log n) vs O(n))
- Skewed tree: BFS wins (O(1) per level vs O(n) recursion)

**When to use BFS**

**1. Shortest path in unweighted graph**
- Guarantees minimum hops
- Track distance and parent

**2. Minimum steps to reach target**
- Word ladder, transformations

**3. Level-order traversal**
- Tree level by level

**4. All nodes within distance K**
- Stop at depth K

**5. Bipartite check**
- Alternate colors level by level

**6. Web crawler within N hops**

**When to use DFS**

**1. Path enumeration**
- Find any or all paths
- Backtracking-friendly

**2. Cycle detection**
- Directed: 3-color (WHITE/GRAY/BLACK)
- Back edge to GRAY = cycle

**3. Topological sort**
- Postorder, then reverse
- Or Kahn's BFS

**4. Connected components**
- Each unvisited start = new component

**5. Strongly connected components**
- Tarjan's, Kosaraju's

**6. Maze / N-queens / Sudoku**
- Classic backtracking

**7. Tree problems**
- Subtree sums, heights, LCA

**Don't use DFS for shortest path**
- DFS finds A path, not THE shortest
- Even on unweighted graphs

**For weighted shortest path**
- Dijkstra (BFS + priority queue) for non-negative
- Bellman-Ford for negative weights
- Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs (small V)

**Implementations — Java**

**BFS tree**
```java
Queue<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
q.offer(root);
while (!q.isEmpty()) {
    TreeNode n = q.poll();
    visit(n);
    if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
    if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
}
```

**BFS graph (with cycle protection)**
```java
Set<Integer> visited = new HashSet<>();
Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
q.offer(start);
visited.add(start);
while (!q.isEmpty()) {
    int node = q.poll();
    for (int next : adj.get(node)) {
        if (visited.add(next)) q.offer(next);
    }
}
```

**DFS recursive**
```java
void dfs(int node, Set<Integer> visited) {
    if (!visited.add(node)) return;
    visit(node);
    for (int next : adj.get(node)) dfs(next, visited);
}
```

**DFS iterative**
```java
Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push(start);
while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
    int node = stack.pop();
    if (!visited.add(node)) continue;
    visit(node);
    for (int next : adj.get(node)) stack.push(next);
}
```

**Always use ArrayDeque**
- Faster than LinkedList for queue
- Faster than legacy Stack class

**Advanced variants**

**Bidirectional BFS**
- Search from both source and target
- Meet in middle
- O(b^(d/2)) instead of O(b^d)
- Huge speedup for large graphs

**Iterative Deepening DFS (IDDFS)**
- DFS with depth limit, repeated
- BFS-like behavior (finds shortest)
- DFS memory (O(d))
- Use for huge search spaces (chess)

**0-1 BFS**
- For edges weighted 0 or 1
- Deque: push 0 to front, 1 to back
- O(V + E)

**A* search**
- BFS + heuristic
- Optimal if heuristic admissible
- Pathfinding in games, robotics

**Dijkstra**
- BFS + priority queue
- Non-negative weighted shortest path
- O((V + E) log V)

**Multi-source BFS**
- Start from multiple sources
- 'Closest of any source' problems

**Common bugs**

**1. Reversed data structures**
- BFS uses queue, DFS uses stack
- Mixing them → wrong order

**2. Forgetting visited set**
- Graph traversal without visited → infinite loop on cycles

**3. DFS for shortest path**
- DFS finds a path, not the shortest
- Use BFS

**4. Stack overflow**
- Deep recursion in DFS
- Use iterative for unknown-depth graphs

**5. OOM on wide BFS**
- Last level can hold n/2 nodes
- Use bidirectional or limit

**6. Wrong cycle detection**
- Undirected: simple visited works
- Directed: need 3-color (back edge to GRAY)

**For interviews**
- BFS shortest path vs DFS path enumeration
- Mention 3-color cycle detection
- Topological sort: DFS postorder reversed
- ArrayDeque for both
- Bidirectional BFS for large-graph shortest path
- Dijkstra as 'BFS + priority queue' for weights

**Recommendation:** Use **BFS** (queue, FIFO) for **shortest path in unweighted graphs**, **level-order traversal**, finding **all nodes within distance K**, **bipartite checks**, and any 'find shortest / minimum steps' problem — the level-by-level expansion guarantees that the first time you reach the target, it's via the shortest path. Use **DFS** (stack or recursion, LIFO) for **path enumeration**, **cycle detection** (3-color WHITE/GRAY/BLACK — back edge to GRAY = cycle), **topological sort** (reverse postorder of DAG), **connected components**, **strongly connected components** (Tarjan/Kosaraju), and **backtracking** problems (mazes, N-queens, Sudoku). Both are **O(V + E)** time, but **memory differs**: BFS is O(W) max width (can be O(n) for wide trees), DFS is O(H) max height (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed). In Java, **always use `ArrayDeque`** for both queue and stack — faster than `LinkedList` and the legacy `Stack` class. **Don't use DFS for shortest path** — it finds *a* path, not *the* shortest. For **weighted shortest path**, use **Dijkstra's algorithm** (BFS with priority queue, non-negative weights), **Bellman-Ford** (negative weights, detects negative cycles), or **Floyd-Warshall** (all-pairs, small V). For **huge graph shortest path**, consider **bidirectional BFS** (meets in middle, O(b^(d/2))) or **A*** (BFS + heuristic). For graph traversal, **always use a `visited` set** to avoid infinite loops on cycles. The mental model: **BFS = explore in layers (good for distance); DFS = go deep then backtrack (good for paths and structure)**. Pick the algorithm based on what the problem asks; the data structure follows.

questions.question: Compare adjacency list and adjacency matrix for representing graphs in Java. Cover space and time trade-offs for sparse vs dense graphs.
questions.title: Graph Representation in Java — Adjacency List vs Matrix Trade-offs
questions.direct_answer: **Adjacency matrix**: a 2D `boolean[V][V]` (or `int[V][V]` for weighted) where `matrix[u][v] = true/weight` if edge exists. **Space O(V²)** regardless of edge count. **Edge lookup O(1)**. **Iterate neighbors O(V)** — must scan the whole row. **Best for dense graphs** (E ~ V²) or when frequent edge-existence checks are needed. **Adjacency list**: a `Map<V, List<V>>` or `List<List<V>>` mapping each vertex to its neighbors. **Space O(V + E)**. **Edge lookup O(degree)** — must scan the neighbor list. **Iterate neighbors O(degree)**. **Best for sparse graphs** (E ~ V) — most real-world graphs (social networks, web, road networks). **Java implementations**: matrix as `int[][]`; list as `Map<Integer, List<Integer>>` (flexible) or `List<List<Integer>>` (when vertices are 0..V-1). **Weighted graphs**: matrix stores weights directly; list stores `(neighbor, weight)` pairs as `List<int[]>` or `Map<Integer, Integer>`. **Edge list**: third option — `List<int[]> edges`, where each edge is `[u, v, weight]`. Compact (O(E)), used by **Kruskal's MST**, **Bellman-Ford**, and graph storage formats. **Decision matrix**: dense graph + frequent edge queries → matrix; sparse graph + traversal-heavy → list; algorithms that iterate edges (Kruskal, Bellman-Ford) → edge list. **Algorithm complexity changes**: BFS/DFS is O(V²) on matrix vs O(V + E) on list — huge difference when E << V². **Real-world**: most graphs are sparse → adjacency list dominates production code.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always defaulting to one representation. Forgetting that matrix is O(V²) space even for sparse graphs. Not knowing edge-list is a third option. Confusing neighbor iteration cost (O(V) on matrix vs O(degree) on list)

sections.content:
| Operation | Adjacency Matrix | Adjacency List | Edge List |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Space** | O(V²) | O(V + E) | O(E) |
| **Add edge** | O(1) | O(1) (push to list) | O(1) (append) |
| **Remove edge** | O(1) | O(degree) | O(E) |
| **Edge exists?** | **O(1)** | O(degree) | O(E) |
| **Iterate neighbors of u** | O(V) | **O(degree)** | O(E) |
| **Iterate all edges** | O(V²) | O(V + E) | **O(E)** |
| **Best for dense graphs** | **Yes** | No | No |
| **Best for sparse graphs** | No (wasteful) | **Yes** | Yes |
| **Java implementation** | `int[V][V]` | `Map<V,List<V>>` or `List<List<V>>` | `List<int[]>` |
| **Cache-friendly** | Yes (contiguous) | Less so (scattered) | Yes |
| **Used by** | Floyd-Warshall, dense algos | BFS, DFS, Dijkstra | Kruskal, Bellman-Ford |

sections.title: Adjacency Matrix — O(V²) Space
Adjacency List — O(V + E) Space
Edge List — The Third Option
Algorithm Complexity Depends on Representation
sections.content:
**BFS / DFS**:
- Adjacency list: O(V + E) — linear in graph size.
- Adjacency matrix: O(V²) — must scan full row for each vertex.
- For sparse graph (E = O(V)): list O(V) vs matrix O(V²) — huge difference.

**Dijkstra's algorithm**:
- With adjacency list + min-heap: O((V + E) log V).
- With adjacency matrix + array: O(V²).
- For dense graphs, matrix version is competitive.

**Floyd-Warshall (all-pairs shortest path)**:
- Requires matrix; O(V³) time, O(V²) space.
- Use only for small V (~ a few hundred).

**Kruskal's MST**:
- Edge list: O(E log E) sort + union-find.
- Adjacency list: convert to edge list first.

**Prim's MST**:
- Adjacency list + min-heap: O(E log V).
- Adjacency matrix + array: O(V²). Better for dense graphs.

**Topological sort**:
- Adjacency list: O(V + E).
- Adjacency matrix: O(V²).

**Bellman-Ford**:
- Edge list: O(V · E).
- Adjacency list also works.

**Connected components / SCC**:
- Adjacency list: O(V + E).
- Adjacency matrix: O(V²).

**Choose representation based on**:
1. **Density** (E vs V²): sparse → list; dense → matrix.
2. **Operation mix**: edge queries → matrix; traversal → list; edge iteration → edge list.
3. **V size**: V ≤ 1000 → matrix often fine; V ≥ 10K → list.
4. **Memory budget**: matrix is O(V²); list is O(V + E).
5. **Algorithm**: Floyd-Warshall demands matrix; Kruskal demands edge list.

**Real-world default**: adjacency list, because most graphs (social networks, web, road, dependencies) are sparse.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Adjacency matrix**: 2D array, O(V²) space, O(1) edge lookup, O(V) neighbor iteration.
- **Adjacency list**: Map or List of Lists, O(V + E) space, O(degree) edge lookup, O(degree) neighbor iteration.
- **Edge list**: List of (u, v, weight), O(E) space, used by Kruskal / Bellman-Ford.
- **Sparse graph**: E ~ V → adjacency list dominant.
- **Dense graph**: E ~ V² → matrix may be reasonable; for V > ~1000, prefer list anyway.
- **Frequent edge queries**: matrix wins (O(1)).
- **Traversal-heavy**: list wins (O(V + E) BFS/DFS vs O(V²)).
- **No built-in graph in Java**: use Map<Integer, List<Integer>> or roll your own.
- **For weighted graphs**: matrix stores weight directly; list stores (neighbor, weight) pairs.
- **CSR (Compressed Sparse Row)**: two flat arrays for adjacency — cache-friendly, used in HPC / graph DBs.
- **Edge list is best for Kruskal, Bellman-Ford, file I/O**.
- **Algorithm complexity changes**: BFS/DFS O(V + E) on list vs O(V²) on matrix.
- **For very large graphs (V > 10⁶)**: matrix infeasible (TB scale); list essential.
- **For graphs with dynamic vertices**: list more flexible.
- **For small dense graphs**: matrix simpler.
- **For interviews**: default to adjacency list unless V is small or queries are dominant.
- **Java-specific**: List<List<Integer>> with vertices 0..V-1 is the cleanest code; Map<Integer, List<Integer>> for sparse vertex IDs.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Three ways to represent a graph**

**1. Adjacency matrix**
- 2D array V × V
- matrix[u][v] = 1 if edge exists
- Space: O(V²)
- Edge lookup: O(1)
- Neighbor iteration: O(V)

**2. Adjacency list**
- Map / List of Lists
- Each vertex has a list of neighbors
- Space: O(V + E)
- Edge lookup: O(degree)
- Neighbor iteration: O(degree)

**3. Edge list**
- List of edges (u, v, weight)
- Space: O(E)
- Used by Kruskal, Bellman-Ford

**Trade-offs**

**Adjacency matrix**

**Pros**
- O(1) edge lookup
- Simple
- Cache-friendly
- Easy for matrix algorithms (Floyd-Warshall)

**Cons**
- O(V²) space — wasteful for sparse
- O(V) neighbor iteration
- For 1M vertices: 4 TB — infeasible

**Use when**
- Dense graph (E ~ V²)
- Frequent edge queries
- Small V (≤ 1000)
- Floyd-Warshall, transitive closure

**Adjacency list**

**Pros**
- O(V + E) space — efficient for sparse
- O(degree) iteration
- Dynamic vertex/edge add/remove
- Standard for BFS, DFS, Dijkstra

**Cons**
- O(degree) edge query
- Less cache-friendly
- Memory overhead (object headers, list overhead in Java)

**Use when**
- Sparse graph (E << V²)
- Real-world graphs (almost always)
- Traversal-heavy
- Large V

**Edge list**

**Pros**
- O(E) space — most compact
- Easy to sort by weight
- Natural for file I/O

**Cons**
- No fast edge lookup
- No fast neighbor iteration
- Convert to list/matrix for BFS/DFS

**Use when**
- Kruskal MST (sort edges)
- Bellman-Ford (relax all edges)
- Storage / file format

**Java implementations**

**Matrix**
```java
int[][] adj = new int[n][n];
adj[u][v] = weight;
adj[v][u] = weight;   // undirected
```

**List**
```java
List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
adj.get(u).add(v);
```

**Map-based list (for sparse vertex IDs)**
```java
Map<Integer, List<Integer>> adj = new HashMap<>();
adj.computeIfAbsent(u, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(v);
```

**Edge list**
```java
List<int[]> edges = new ArrayList<>();
edges.add(new int[]{u, v, weight});
```

**No built-in graph in Java**
- Unlike Python's networkx
- Roll your own with Map/List
- Or use JGraphT library

**Algorithm complexity depends on representation**

**BFS/DFS**
- List: O(V + E)
- Matrix: O(V²)
- For sparse: huge difference

**Dijkstra**
- List + heap: O((V + E) log V)
- Matrix + array: O(V²) (better for dense)

**Floyd-Warshall**
- Requires matrix
- O(V³) time, O(V²) space
- Small V only

**Kruskal**
- Edge list + union-find: O(E log E)

**Prim**
- List + heap: O(E log V)
- Matrix + array: O(V²)

**Decision guide**

- Density: sparse → list; dense → matrix
- Operations: edge query → matrix; traversal → list; edge iteration → edge list
- V size: ≤ 1000 → matrix often fine; ≥ 10K → list
- Memory: budget tight → list
- Algorithm: Floyd-Warshall → matrix; Kruskal → edge list

**Real-world default**
- Adjacency list
- Most graphs (social networks, web, road, dependencies) are sparse

**Advanced: CSR (Compressed Sparse Row)**
- Two flat arrays: offsets[V+1], neighbors[E]
- Cache-friendly
- Used in HPC, graph DBs (e.g., Neo4j, Pregel)
- Half the memory of List<List<Integer>> in Java

**Common bugs**

**1. Always defaulting to one representation**
- Match representation to algorithm

**2. Forgetting matrix is O(V²) for sparse too**
- 1M vertex sparse graph: matrix infeasible, list fine

**3. Confusing iteration cost**
- Matrix neighbor iteration: O(V) per vertex
- List: O(degree) per vertex

**4. Not using adjacency list for Dijkstra**
- Matrix version is O(V²); list + heap is O((V+E) log V)
- For sparse: list wins by a lot

**5. Storing weights wrong in matrix**
- 0 means no edge for unweighted
- For 0-weight edges, use Integer.MAX_VALUE for missing

**6. Forgetting bidirectional add for undirected**
- adj[u][v] AND adj[v][u]
- Or in list: add to both u's and v's lists

**For interviews**

**Default: adjacency list** for most problems
**Matrix**: when V is small and edge queries are frequent
**Edge list**: for Kruskal, Bellman-Ford
**Mention complexity** changes based on representation
**Mention** Java has no built-in graph type

**Recommendation:** **Adjacency list** is the **default** for most graph problems in Java because real-world graphs are **sparse** (social networks, web, road networks, dependencies) and **O(V + E)** space scales to billions of edges. **Adjacency matrix** is preferred when (1) the graph is **dense** (E ~ V²), (2) **edge-existence queries are frequent** (O(1) vs O(degree)), (3) **V is small** (≤ 1000) so O(V²) is manageable, or (4) the algorithm requires it (**Floyd-Warshall** for all-pairs shortest path). **Edge list** is the choice for **Kruskal's MST** (sort by weight) and **Bellman-Ford** (relax all edges), and is the natural format for file I/O. **Java has no built-in graph type** — use `List<List<Integer>>` (when vertices are 0..V-1) or `Map<Integer, List<Integer>>` (sparse vertex IDs); for weighted edges, use `List<int[]>` or a `record Edge(int to, int weight)`. **Algorithm complexity changes dramatically** with representation: BFS/DFS is **O(V + E)** on adjacency list but **O(V²)** on matrix — for sparse graphs, the difference is massive (e.g., 10⁶ vs 10¹² operations for V=10⁶). **Dijkstra** on list + heap is O((V+E) log V); on matrix + array, it's O(V²) (competitive for dense graphs). For **very large graphs**, consider **CSR (Compressed Sparse Row)** — two flat arrays (offsets + neighbors) that's cache-friendly and half the memory of `List<List<Integer>>`. The mental model: **matrix = bitmap (fast lookup, dense storage); list = sparse map (efficient for traversal); edge list = compact catalog (good for sorting)**. Pick based on **density, operations, and the algorithm you'll run**; default to **adjacency list** if uncertain.

questions.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm in Java — Shortest Path with PriorityQueue
questions.direct_answer: **Dijkstra's algorithm** finds the **shortest path from a source to all other vertices** in a **weighted graph with non-negative edge weights**. It greedily picks the **unvisited vertex with the smallest known distance**, **relaxes** all its edges (updates neighbor distances if a shorter path is found), and repeats. **Time complexity**: **O((V + E) log V)** using a binary heap (PriorityQueue) and adjacency list — the standard in Java. **O(V²)** with an array (better only for dense graphs). **O(E + V log V)** with a Fibonacci heap (theoretical; rarely implemented). **Space**: O(V) for distance array + O(V) for heap. **Algorithm steps**: (1) initialize all distances to infinity, source to 0; (2) push (0, source) onto a min-heap keyed by distance; (3) repeatedly pop the smallest; (4) for each popped vertex, **skip if already finalized** (lazy deletion handles stale heap entries); (5) for each neighbor, if `dist[u] + weight < dist[v]`, update `dist[v]` and push `(dist[v], v)`. **Java implementation**: use `PriorityQueue<int[]>` with comparator on the first element. **Limitations**: (1) **Doesn't work with negative weights** — the greedy choice is invalid; use **Bellman-Ford** instead. (2) Doesn't handle negative cycles. **Variants**: (a) **A***: Dijkstra + heuristic, faster for known-target search; (b) **Bidirectional Dijkstra**: meet-in-the-middle for huge graphs; (c) **0-1 BFS**: special case for weights only 0 or 1, uses deque, O(V + E). **Common bug**: not skipping stale heap entries, leading to O(V² log V) due to redundant relaxation. **Real-world use**: GPS navigation (Google Maps uses contraction hierarchies), network routing (OSPF), and game pathfinding (with A*).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can implement Dijkstra correctly using PriorityQueue, knows complexity O((V+E) log V), understands the lazy-deletion pattern, and knows the no-negative-weights limitation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not handling stale heap entries (re-processing visited vertices). Using on graphs with negative weights. Forgetting the visited / finalized set. Using LinkedList for the heap (slow). Not initializing distances to MAX_VALUE
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Bellman-Ford for negative weights, A* with heuristic, bidirectional Dijkstra for huge graphs, the priority queue's lazy-deletion trick, and real-world systems (Google Maps contraction hierarchies)

sections.title: What Dijkstra Solves
sections.content:
**Single-source shortest path** in a **weighted directed or undirected graph** with **non-negative edge weights**.

**Input**: graph G = (V, E), source vertex s, edge weights w(u, v) ≥ 0.

**Output**: shortest distance from s to every other vertex (and optionally the path itself).

**Greedy invariant**: at each step, the algorithm **finalizes** the distance to the closest unfinalized vertex. Once finalized, the distance is guaranteed correct — no future relaxation can improve it.

**Why non-negative weights are required**: with negative weights, a vertex you've finalized might be improved later via a negative edge. Dijkstra's greedy choice fails. Use **Bellman-Ford** for negative weights.

**Why O((V + E) log V)**:
- Each vertex pushed to heap O(E) times (once per edge in the worst case with lazy deletion).
- Each heap operation: O(log V).
- Total: O((V + E) log V).

**Use cases**:
- **GPS navigation**: shortest route by distance / time.
- **Network routing**: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) protocol.
- **Game AI pathfinding**: Dijkstra (or A* for heuristic guidance).
- **Supply chain**: cheapest delivery route.
- **Word ladders with weighted transitions**.

**Comparison with BFS**:
- BFS: shortest path in **unweighted** graph, O(V + E).
- Dijkstra: shortest path in **weighted (non-negative)** graph, O((V + E) log V).
- Dijkstra reduces to BFS when all weights are 1.

sections.title: Java Implementation — PriorityQueue + Adjacency List
Why Lazy Deletion Works
sections.content:
**Problem**: Java's `PriorityQueue` doesn't support efficient **decrease-key**. When we find a shorter distance to `v`, we can't update an existing heap entry in O(log V); removal is O(n).

**Solution: lazy deletion**:
- Just push the new (shorter, v) entry; don't remove the old one.
- When we pop (d, u), check if `d > dist[u]`. If so, this is a **stale** entry from before a better path was found; skip it.
- The valid entry (with the current best dist[u]) will be popped later, before any longer-distance entry for u.

**Correctness**:
- Heap pops smallest first.
- When we first pop (d, u) with d == dist[u], we've found the optimal distance to u.
- Any later pop with the same u has d ≥ current dist[u], hence stale.

**Complexity analysis with lazy deletion**:
- Each edge can trigger one push: O(E) total pushes.
- Each push and pop: O(log V).
- Total: O((V + E) log V) = O(E log V) for connected graph.

**Alternative: use TreeSet for true decrease-key**:
```java
TreeSet<int[]> tset = new TreeSet<>((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? a[0] - b[0] : a[1] - b[1]);
// remove old entry
tset.remove(new int[]{oldDist, v});
tset.add(new int[]{newDist, v});
```
- O(log V) per operation including removal.
- Total: O((V + E) log V) — same big-O but more constant factor.
- Lazy deletion is simpler and often faster in practice.

**Don't use Stack or LinkedList**:
- LinkedList offers O(1) head ops, but no priority semantics.
- Stack: LIFO, not min-heap.
- Always use PriorityQueue (binary heap) or TreeSet.

sections.title: Variants — A*, Bidirectional, 0-1 BFS
sections.content:
**A* algorithm**: Dijkstra + heuristic h(v) estimating remaining distance to target.
```java
pq.offer(new int[]{f(v), v});   // f(v) = g(v) + h(v)
```
Where g(v) = current known distance, h(v) = estimated remaining (admissible: never overestimates).

**Use case**: pathfinding with a known target; e.g., game maps, GPS.

**If h(v) = 0**: A* reduces to Dijkstra.

**Common heuristics**:
- **Manhattan distance**: |x1-x2| + |y1-y2| for grid with 4-direction movement.
- **Euclidean distance**: √((x1-x2)² + (y1-y2)²) for any-direction movement.
- **Domain-specific**: lower bound from problem structure.

**Bidirectional Dijkstra**:
- Run two Dijkstras: forward from source, backward from target.
- Stop when they meet.
- Speedup factor: 2 (theoretical, often more in practice).
- Use case: shortest path in huge static graphs (road networks).

**0-1 BFS**:
- Special case: edge weights are only 0 or 1.
- Use deque instead of priority queue.
- Push 0-weight edges to front, 1-weight to back.
- Time: O(V + E).

**Multi-source Dijkstra**:
- Initialize all sources with distance 0.
- Push all sources onto heap.
- 'Closest of any source' problem.

**Real-world: contraction hierarchies (Google Maps)**:
- Preprocess graph: rank vertices by importance, add 'shortcut' edges.
- Query time: 1000× faster than plain Dijkstra on continental road networks.
- Used by OSRM, Graphhopper.

**Don't use Dijkstra**:
- For negative weights: use Bellman-Ford (O(V · E)).
- For DAG with weights: topological sort + relaxation (O(V + E)).
- For all-pairs: Floyd-Warshall (O(V³)).

sections.title: Limitations and When NOT to Use Dijkstra
sections.content:
**1. Negative weights** — Dijkstra fails.
```
A --(-5)--> B
A --(2)--> C --(2)--> B
```
Dijkstra finalizes A->C->B = 4, never reconsiders A->B = -5. Use **Bellman-Ford** (O(V · E)) which handles negatives and detects negative cycles.

**2. Negative cycle** — no shortest path exists (can keep going around).
- Bellman-Ford detects this: after V-1 iterations, if any edge can still relax, there's a negative cycle.

**3. Very large graphs** — plain Dijkstra is too slow.
- Use bidirectional Dijkstra, A*, or contraction hierarchies.
- For continental road networks: contraction hierarchies preprocess once, queries are sub-millisecond.

**4. Frequent updates** — dynamic graph.
- Recompute from scratch is O((V + E) log V) per update.
- Use incremental algorithms (rare in practice).

**5. All-pairs shortest path**:
- Floyd-Warshall: O(V³), works for any weights without negative cycles.
- Run Dijkstra from each vertex: O(V · (V + E) log V), better for sparse graphs.
- Johnson's algorithm: O(V · E log V) using reweighting (Bellman-Ford to remove negatives).

**6. Weights changing during search** — algorithm assumes static graph.

**7. K-shortest paths** — use Yen's algorithm or Eppstein's.

**8. Constrained shortest path** (e.g., 'shortest with at most K edges'):
- Bellman-Ford variant: dp[k][v] = shortest distance with at most k edges.

**Bellman-Ford comparison**:
- Time: O(V · E) — slower than Dijkstra.
- Handles negative weights.
- Detects negative cycles.
- Used in distance-vector routing protocols (RIP).

**Don't reinvent**:
- For production: use a library like JGraphT or Guava's graph package.
- For interviews: implement Dijkstra by hand to demonstrate understanding.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Dijkstra**: single-source shortest path in weighted graph with **non-negative weights**.
- **Greedy**: finalize closest unvisited vertex; once finalized, distance is correct.
- **Time**: O((V + E) log V) with binary heap (Java's PriorityQueue) + adjacency list.
- O(V²) with array (better for dense graphs).
- O(E + V log V) with Fibonacci heap (theoretical).
- **Space**: O(V) for distances + O(V) for heap.
- **Java**: use `PriorityQueue<int[]>` keyed by distance; lazy deletion.
- **Lazy deletion**: skip stale entries with `if (d > dist[u]) continue;` because Java's PQ has no efficient decrease-key.
- **Initialization**: distances to MAX_VALUE; source to 0.
- **Avoid integer overflow**: check `dist[u] != MAX_VALUE` before adding weight, or use `long`.
- **Doesn't work with negative weights** — greedy fails.
- **For negatives**: Bellman-Ford (O(V · E)), detects negative cycles.
- **For DAGs**: topological sort + relaxation (O(V + E)).
- **For all-pairs**: Floyd-Warshall (O(V³)) or Johnson's (O(V · E log V)).
- **Variants**: A* (with heuristic), bidirectional Dijkstra, 0-1 BFS, multi-source.
- **Real-world**: GPS (contraction hierarchies), routing (OSPF), game pathfinding (A*).
- **For interviews**: implement Dijkstra cold; mention lazy deletion, Bellman-Ford for negatives, A* for known target.
- **Path reconstruction**: maintain parent[] array; trace from target back to source.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Dijkstra's algorithm — what it does**

- Single-source shortest path
- Weighted graph
- **Non-negative weights** (critical limitation)

**Algorithm**

**1. Initialize**
- All distances = infinity
- dist[source] = 0
- Push (0, source) onto min-heap

**2. Loop**
- Pop (d, u) — the smallest distance
- If d > dist[u]: stale entry, skip
- Else: relax all outgoing edges
  - For each (v, weight): if d + weight < dist[v], update and push

**3. Continue** until heap empty

**Greedy invariant**
- At each step, finalize the closest unvisited vertex
- Once finalized, distance is correct
- No future relaxation can improve it
- Why non-negative weights matter: negative would invalidate this

**Java implementation**

```java
int[] dist = new int[n];
Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
dist[source] = 0;

PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(
    Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[0])
);
pq.offer(new int[]{0, source});

while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
    int[] cur = pq.poll();
    int d = cur[0], u = cur[1];
    if (d > dist[u]) continue;   // lazy deletion
    for (int[] edge : adj.get(u)) {
        int v = edge[0], w = edge[1];
        int newDist = d + w;
        if (newDist < dist[v]) {
            dist[v] = newDist;
            pq.offer(new int[]{newDist, v});
        }
    }
}
```

**Complexity**

**With binary heap (Java's PQ) + adjacency list**
- O((V + E) log V)
- Standard implementation

**With array + matrix**
- O(V²)
- Better for dense graphs

**With Fibonacci heap**
- O(E + V log V)
- Theoretical; rarely implemented

**Lazy deletion explained**

**Problem**
- Java's PriorityQueue has no efficient decrease-key
- Removing arbitrary element is O(n)

**Solution**
- Just push duplicate entries when you find a shorter path
- When popping, check if d > dist[u]; if so, skip
- Stale entries are 'lazily deleted' by being ignored

**Correctness**
- Heap pops smallest first
- First time we pop (d, u) with d == dist[u]: that's the final answer
- Later pops with same u have d ≥ dist[u]: stale, skip

**Total complexity**
- O(E) pushes total (one per edge in worst case)
- O(log V) per operation
- O((V + E) log V)

**Limitations**

**1. Negative weights**
- Dijkstra fails
- Greedy choice invalid
- Use Bellman-Ford (O(V · E))

**2. Negative cycle**
- No shortest path (loop forever)
- Bellman-Ford detects this

**3. Very large graphs**
- Use bidirectional Dijkstra, A*, contraction hierarchies

**4. Frequent graph updates**
- Recompute is expensive
- Static graphs are the sweet spot

**Variants**

**A***
- Dijkstra + heuristic
- f(v) = g(v) + h(v)
- Faster for known target
- Manhattan / Euclidean distance heuristics
- Used in games, GPS

**Bidirectional Dijkstra**
- Forward from source + backward from target
- Meet in middle
- ~2× faster
- Useful for huge graphs

**0-1 BFS**
- Special case: weights only 0 or 1
- Use deque
- Push 0-weight to front, 1-weight to back
- O(V + E)

**Multi-source Dijkstra**
- Init all sources with distance 0
- Push all to heap
- 'Closest of any source' problems

**Contraction hierarchies (real world)**
- Preprocess: rank vertices, add shortcut edges
- Query: 1000× faster
- Used by Google Maps, OSRM, Graphhopper
- Continental road networks: sub-millisecond queries

**Path reconstruction**
```java
int[] parent = new int[n];
Arrays.fill(parent, -1);
// In relaxation:
parent[v] = u;
// Reconstruct:
List<Integer> path = new ArrayList<>();
for (int c = target; c != -1; c = parent[c]) path.add(c);
Collections.reverse(path);
```

**Common bugs**

**1. Not handling stale entries**
- Without lazy deletion check: wastes work, but still correct
- With check: optimal

**2. Using on negative weights**
- Wrong answer
- Use Bellman-Ford

**3. Integer overflow**
- d + weight can overflow if d == MAX_VALUE
- Check dist[u] != MAX_VALUE first
- Or use long

**4. Forgetting bidirectional add for undirected**
- Add to both u's and v's adjacency lists

**5. Wrong PQ ordering**
- Must be MIN-heap
- Default Java PQ is min-heap when using natural order
- Comparator: comparingInt(a -> a[0])

**6. Using LinkedList or Stack**
- LinkedList: no priority semantics
- Stack: LIFO, not min
- Use PriorityQueue (binary heap) or TreeSet

**Compared to other algorithms**

**BFS**
- Unweighted shortest path
- O(V + E)
- Dijkstra reduces to BFS when all weights = 1

**Bellman-Ford**
- Negative weights OK
- O(V · E)
- Detects negative cycles
- Used in RIP routing protocol

**Floyd-Warshall**
- All-pairs shortest path
- O(V³)
- Works for any weights without negative cycles
- Small V only

**A***
- Dijkstra + heuristic
- Optimal if heuristic admissible
- Faster for known target

**For interviews**
- Implement Dijkstra cold
- Use PriorityQueue + lazy deletion
- Mention O((V + E) log V)
- Address no-negative-weights limitation
- Mention Bellman-Ford for negatives, A* for known target, bidirectional for huge graphs

**Recommendation:** Implement **Dijkstra's algorithm** in Java using **`PriorityQueue<int[]>`** keyed by distance and an **adjacency list** — this gives you **O((V + E) log V)** time, which is the standard for sparse graphs. Use the **lazy deletion pattern** (skip with `if (d > dist[u]) continue;`) because Java's PriorityQueue doesn't support efficient decrease-key; just push duplicate entries when you find shorter paths and ignore stale ones when popping. **Initialize distances to `Integer.MAX_VALUE`** and source to 0; **avoid integer overflow** by checking `dist[u] != MAX_VALUE` before adding weight, or use `long`. The **critical limitation**: Dijkstra **does not work with negative edge weights** — the greedy 'finalize closest' invariant breaks. For negative weights, use **Bellman-Ford** (O(V · E), detects negative cycles); for DAGs use **topological sort + relaxation** (O(V + E)); for all-pairs use **Floyd-Warshall** (O(V³)) or **Johnson's** (O(V · E log V)); for graphs with weights only 0 or 1, **0-1 BFS** with a deque achieves O(V + E). For **known-target search**, use **A*** with an admissible heuristic (Manhattan, Euclidean) for big speedups. For **huge static graphs** (continental road networks), use **contraction hierarchies** — preprocess once, query in sub-millisecond (used by Google Maps, OSRM, Graphhopper). For **path reconstruction**, maintain a `parent[]` array and trace backward from target. The mental model: **Dijkstra = greedy expansion from cheapest frontier; valid because finalizing the closest vertex is always safe with non-negative weights**. For interviews, **implement it cold**, mention the **lazy deletion trick**, the **negative-weight limitation**, and gracefully transition to **Bellman-Ford / A* / contraction hierarchies** when asked about variants.
